title: Phonics and sound symbol correspondences flash cards

cards.front: Which letter group gives /u/ in sous?
back: ou.

cards.front: Which vowel is different from ou in dur?
back: u.

cards.front: What sound does qu usually make?
What sound does French th make?
What sound does ç make?
Which final verb letters are silent in ils parlent?
back: -ent.

cards.front: Does the h in homme make an English h sound?
back: No.

cards.front: What linking sound can final s make in les amis?
What linking sound can final x make in deux amis?
What linking sound is heard in petit ami?
What consonant links in un ami?
Which sound group appears at the end of travail?
back: -ail, /aj/.

cards.front: Explain how your mouth position differs for u and ou.
back: U: tongue forward, lips rounded.
Ou: tongue further back, lips rounded.

cards.front: Explain what a nasal vowel means for grand.
back: Some air passes through the nose. Do not add a separate strong n after its /ɑ̃/ vowel.

cards.front: Give two spellings that can represent the /o/ sound in beau.
back: Au and eau. Closed o/ô can also represent it.

cards.front: Explain the pronunciation of infinitive parler and vous parlez endings.
back: Both endings normally give /e/. Their different written endings still show different grammatical forms.

cards.front: Why is ville an important exception when learning -ille?
back: Ville has an /l/ sound, while words such as famille commonly have /j/. Not every -ille word follows one rule.

cards.front: Explain why a single s differs in maison and chanson.
back: In maison it lies between vowel sounds and is usually /z/. In chanson it is followed by a consonant and is /s/.

cards.front: Explain the difference between bon and bonne.
back: Bon has a nasal vowel; bonne has a pronounced n and a non-nasal vowel. The doubled consonant changes the sound pattern.

cards.front: Explain why et amis should not be read with a linking t.
back: There is no liaison after **et**, even though the next word starts with a vowel.

cards.front: What changes between les hommes and les héros?
back: Les hommes allows /z/ liaison. Héros has an h aspiré, which blocks liaison; neither h is pronounced like English h.

cards.front: Compare French ch and j.
back: Ch is /ʃ/ as in chose; j is voiced /ʒ/ as in jeunesse.

cards.front: Identify the sound groups in beau, matin and campagne.
back: Beau: eau, /o/.
Matin: in, /ɛ̃/.
Campagne: gn, /ɲ/.

cards.front: Identify the sound groups in cœur, porte and application.
back: Cœur: open œu, /œ/.
Porte: open o, /ɔ/.
Application: -tion, /sjɔ̃/.

cards.front: Explain three pronunciation checks for Les petits enfants jouent.
back: No liaison between les and petits, because petits starts with a consonant.
Petits enfants can link with /z/.
The verb ending -ent in jouent is silent.

cards.front: Why can je parle, tu parles and ils parlent sound similar, but require different spellings?
back: Regular -e/-es/-ent endings can be silent.
The subject identifies the person and number.
Written agreement is still required even when it is not audible.

cards.front: A learner says every final consonant is silent and every vowel-starting next word causes liaison. Correct both claims with examples.
back: Many final consonants are silent, but **avec** has a final /k/.
Some final r sounds are heard, as in **partir**.
Liaison depends on the word combination: **les amis** allows it.
**Et amis** has no liaison after et.

cards.front: Explain four checks when writing a sentence from dictation.
back: Match letter groups to the heard vowel and consonant sounds.
Separate liaison sounds from the next word's spelling.
Use the subject to recover silent verb endings.
Check noun/adjective number and gender, including silent endings.
